whatItIs.text: A yeast-leavened round flatbread of wheat, water, yeast, and salt — the pocketed kind puffs into two layers in a very hot oven; in Greece 'pita' still means the thick, pocketless kind.

historyNote.text: Pita's roots run to prehistoric flatbreads: the Natufian people of Jordan were baking wild-cereal flatbread about 14,500 years ago, and Babylonian cooks baked pita-like loaves in tannur ovens 4,000 years ago — though the steam-puffed pocket version is probably younger, since no ancient text or medieval Arab cookbook records it.

howToChoose.text: Look for soft, flexible breads without dry, cracking edges; wholegrain versions hold fillings better, and very fresh pitas reheat beautifully.

storage.text: Keep at room temperature in a sealed bag for a day or two, or freeze — the fridge dries bread fastest. The rulebook has the details.
storage.note: bread storage windows live in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: A day-old pita crisps into chips with oil and za'atar, toasts for breakfast, or splits for last-minute sandwiches; stale ones tear into soups and fattoush.

substitutions.note: thinner, no pocket; wraps instead of pockets
